sections.h2: What should I know before selling a house in Ithaca, NY?
sections.html:
Ithaca is a university city where renters outnumber owners, so the first question for most sellers is whether the house has ever been a rental. The Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied rate at 29.6% for 2020-2024, with 14,167 households and an average of 1.71 people each, and that mix shapes both the buyer pool and the city paperwork.

The city sits at the south end of Cayuga Lake in Tompkins County, and the surrounding Town of Ithaca is a legally separate municipality, so confirm which one covers your address. Estimated population on July 1, 2025 was 33,632, a gain of 4.8% from the 2020 base of 32,085. Only 54.2% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, which shows how often households here turn over. A seller should decide early whether the likely buyer is an owner-occupant, an investor who wants rental income, or a cash buyer who will take the house as it stands.

  • Owner-occupied houses on East Hill, West Hill and South Hill usually sell to buyers who plan to live in them.
  • Houses near Collegetown or with accessory apartments draw investors, who will ask about the rental certificate.
  • Houses that need work or carry tenants may sell fastest to a buyer who pays cash.

sections.h2: How is Ithaca laid out, and why does it matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Ithaca was built on flat land at the south end of Cayuga Lake and then spread up three hillsides: East Hill, West Hill and South Hill. Cornell University sits on East Hill, between the Fall Creek and Cascadilla Creek gorges, and Ithaca College moved to South Hill in the 1960s.

That terrain gives the city steep streets, creek gorges and older frame houses on small lots. A seller on a hillside lot should expect questions about drainage, retaining walls and winter access. Buyers coming from outside the area often ask about driving, and Wikipedia notes that every trip into Ithaca involves two-lane state highways, with the city sitting at the junction of Routes 13, 13A, 34, 79, 89, 96, 96B and 366. New York City is about 225 miles away, and Binghamton and Syracuse are each roughly an hour by car.

Education drives the local economy. Cornell opened in 1865 and Ithaca College began in 1892 as a conservatory, and the Ithaca City School District, which Wikipedia describes as serving about 5,500 students, covers the city and the area around it. Collegetown, next to the Cornell campus, has seen many new apartment buildings, and the Ithaca Commons pedestrian mall anchors the downtown.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers show for Ithaca home values and rents?
sections.html:
The median value of an owner-occupied home in the city is $342,700 for 2020-2024, and median gross rent is $1,447. Median monthly owner costs are $2,368 with a mortgage and $994 without one.

Household income is $48,784 at the median, and per-capita income is $31,599, while 67.7% of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher. The poverty rate is 30.4%, a figure shaped by the large student population. Because the city's land area is only 5.39 square miles and the 2020 density was 5,958 people per square mile, the housing stock is tight, and even a modest house can draw several showings in a good season.

Mean travel time to work is 18.7 minutes. That short commute, plus the Cornell and Ithaca College job base, is why buyers pay attention to walkable addresses. Retail and food-service sales per Census data give a sense of the city's visitor economy: accommodation and food services totaled about $200 million in 2022.

sections.h2: What does the City of Ithaca require for rental housing and short-term rentals?
sections.html:
The City requires a housing inspection and a Certificate of Compliance for residential rental dwellings, and a buyer who plans to rent the property will check that the certificate is current. The rule covers one- and two-family dwellings, multiple dwellings, dormitories, fraternities, sororities, mixed-use buildings with residential units and accessory apartments in single-family homes.

Fees depend on the building type. The Building Division bills the property owner once the inspection is done, and payment is due within 30 days. Owners get one 30-day extension per property to prepare for an inspection or to fix violations without added violation charges.

Short-term rentals add a permit on top of the Certificate of Compliance. The city's host guide says the permit lasts one year, the permit number must appear in every listing, a local contact must respond within 60 minutes, and hosts collect both a Tompkins County and a City of Ithaca hotel room occupancy tax, each at 5%. If a buyer is purchasing your house as a short-term rental, ask the Building Division at 108 E. Green Street whether the permit transfers or must be reissued. The division's phone line for housing inspections is (607) 274-6509.

sections.h2: How is a deed recorded in Tompkins County, and what does it cost?
sections.html:
The Tompkins County Clerk is the registrar of deeds for Ithaca, and the clerk's published schedule lists the first page of a deed at $50 with each added page at $5. A $10 deed notice applies to residential deeds recorded since March 11, 2020, and the TP-584 transfer tax return costs $5.

The clerk lists the transfer tax as $6 per $1,000. The RP-5217 real property transfer report carries a $125 fee when the property is residential and $250 otherwise. Sellers who live out of state must file form IT-2663, which the state revises every year, so a printed copy from an earlier year will not do. Payment at the clerk's counter is by cash or check.

Searching land records costs $5 per name for records back to 1968 when clerk staff perform the search, and copies are $0.65 a page with a $1.30 minimum. For a seller, the practical point is that the closing attorney or title company handles these filings, but it helps to know that Tompkins County's numbers differ from Suffolk or Chautauqua County, so a settlement statement copied from a past sale elsewhere in New York will not match.

sections.h2: How do winters and gorges affect an Ithaca house sale?
sections.html:
Ithaca averages about 67 inches of snow a year, and frost can arrive at any time except midsummer. The average first freeze is October 5 and the last is May 15, which gives the area a 141-day growing season and a USDA hardiness zone between 5b and 6a.

Inspectors look closely at roofs, gutters, foundations and heating systems in a climate like this. A buyer will ask the age of the furnace, whether pipes in exterior walls have frozen, and how water drains off the lot after spring melt. Summers are warm and brief, with afternoon thunderstorms and the occasional heat wave that reaches the mid-90s to 100 degrees, so a house with no cooling is still sellable but may prompt a lower offer.

  • Gather heating, roof and foundation records before the first showing.
  • Photograph the house in a dry season if the basement ever took on water.
  • Clear gutters and walkways before an inspection in the colder months.

sections.h2: Is a cash offer a good fit for an Ithaca house?
sections.html:
A cash offer fits when the house has rental violations, deferred repairs or tenants in place, since those problems slow a financed sale. For a clean owner-occupied house in a desirable neighborhood, an open-market listing may bring more.

Get any offer in writing, ask how the buyer handles an expired Certificate of Compliance or open violations, and confirm that a New York real estate attorney will review the contract. Compare the price with what you would net after commission, repairs and carrying costs over several months. Selling a student rental also raises timing questions, so ask the buyer in advance how existing leases would be handled.

faqs.q: Does Ithaca require a certificate before I sell a rental house?
faqs.a: The city requires a Certificate of Compliance for residential rental dwellings, issued after a housing inspection by the Building Division. A buyer who intends to keep renting will usually want it current, so schedule the inspection early. The division accepts inspection applications online.

faqs.q: How much is a Certificate of Compliance for a one-family house in Ithaca?
faqs.a: The initial inspection fee is $100 for a one-family dwelling and $175 for a two-family dwelling. Each violation found adds $10, and each violation still uncorrected at re-inspection costs $50. A return trip is billed at $75 per hour with a $75 minimum.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in Tompkins County?
faqs.a: The Tompkins County Clerk charges $50 for the first page of a deed and $5 for each added page. Add a $10 deed notice, a $5 TP-584 filing and the RP-5217 fee of $125 for residential property. The clerk lists the transfer tax at $6 per $1,000.

faqs.q: How many people live in the City of Ithaca?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau estimates 33,632 residents as of July 1, 2025. That is up 4.8% from the 2020 base. The city covers 5.39 square miles of land.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Ithaca house if it has an Airbnb permit?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask the Building Division whether a new owner has to apply for a fresh permit. The permit lasts one year, it depends on a current Certificate of Compliance, and hosts collect separate 5% city and county occupancy taxes.
